title: The Gut-Brain Connection in Kids: Can Food Really Help Heal the Mind?
author: THE FOOD MATTERS TEAM
content:
In today’s world, more children than ever are struggling with their mental health. ADHD, anxiety, depression, autism spectrum disorders—these conditions are on the rise, leaving parents searching for answers that go beyond prescriptions and quick fixes. What if one of the most powerful tools to support a child’s emotional and mental wellbeing is something as simple—and profound—as what’s on their plate?
Welcome to the gut-brain connection: a revolutionary shift in how we understand children’s mental health. And yes, food really can help heal the mind.
Did you know your child has two brains?
Not in the science-fiction sense, of course. But the gut—home to trillions of microbes—is so rich in neurons and so closely linked to the brain that scientists call it the “second brain.” This gut-brain axis is a two-way communication highway, and what happens in the gut can directly influence mood, focus, and behavior.
This means that inflammation in the digestive tract, imbalanced gut bacteria, or food sensitivities might not just show up as tummy troubles. They can show up as mood swings, anxiety, poor concentration, even sleep issues.
More and more research is confirming what functional medicine experts like Dr. Mark Hyman and Dr. Tom O’Bryan have been saying for years: food isn’t just fuel—it’s information.
Certain foods can send calming, healing messages to the body and brain. Others can trigger inflammation, stress hormones, and neurochemical imbalances.
Here's how food influences mental health in children:
Ultra-Processed Foods & Sugar: Linked to mood instability, aggression, and brain fog. Many ultra-processed foods also harm the gut microbiome.
Artificial Dyes & Additives: Common in kids’ snacks and cereals, these have been associated with increased hyperactivity and behavioral issues.
Gluten & Dairy Sensitivities: In some children, these can contribute to leaky gut and neuroinflammation, which may worsen symptoms of ADHD or anxiety.
Omega-3 Fats: Found in wild fish, flaxseeds, and walnuts, these healthy fats are crucial for brain development and mood regulation.
Protein: Found in lean meats, dairy, nuts, seeds, fish and legumes, protein supports the gut-brain axis by providing essential amino acids that fuel neurotransmitter production, helping regulate mood, focus, and behavior in children.
Fermented Foods & Probiotics: These nourish beneficial gut bacteria, supporting a healthy microbiome—and a more balanced mind.
The gut microbiome—the ecosystem of bacteria living in the digestive system—plays a key role in producing neurotransmitters like serotonin, dopamine, and GABA, which directly affect mood and focus. In fact, about 90% of serotonin is produced in the gut.
When a child’s microbiome is imbalanced (a condition called dysbiosis), it can lead to emotional dysregulation, irritability, and even symptoms that mimic psychiatric disorders.

Even small shifts can make a big difference in a child’s behavior, sleep, and emotional regulation.
Of course, food is just one piece of the puzzle. A truly holistic approach to mental health also includes:
What this new wave of research and clinical experience is showing us is deeply empowering: mental health is not set in stone. And for children, especially, the earlier we intervene with supportive nutrition and lifestyle choices, the more profound the healing can be.
Food is not the whole answer—but it is a powerful place to begin. Because when we nourish a child’s body, we also nourish their mind. title: Is Your Gut Whispering for Help? When to Consider Testing for SIBO
author: THE FOOD MATTERS TEAM
content:
We understand that sometimes, despite our best efforts with diet and lifestyle, our gut health can still feel… off. If you’ve been experiencing persistent digestive woes that don’t seem to have a clear cause, Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO) might be worth investigating.
As the name suggests, SIBO is a condition where there’s an excessive amount of bacteria in the small intestine. This overgrowth can interfere with nutrient absorption, damage the intestinal lining, and lead to a cascade of uncomfortable symptoms.
But how do you know if your gut whispers are actually a call for SIBO testing? It’s important to note that only a qualified healthcare practitioner can diagnose SIBO, and testing should be guided by their professional opinion.
However, understanding the common signs and situations where SIBO is more likely can empower you to have informed conversations with your doctor.
Listen to Your Gut: Key Symptoms That Might Point to SIBO
While digestive issues are common, certain patterns and combinations of symptoms can raise suspicion for SIBO:
Persistent Bloating: Feeling constantly bloated, especially after meals, even small ones. This bloating often feels significant and uncomfortable.
Excessive Gas: Frequent and excessive flatulence or belching.
Abdominal Pain or Discomfort: Cramping, pain, or a general feeling of unease in your abdomen.
Changes in Bowel Habits: This can manifest as diarrhea, constipation, or alternating between the two.
Food Intolerances: Developing new sensitivities to previously well-tolerated foods, particularly those high in fermentable carbohydrates (FODMAPs).
Nutrient Deficiencies: Despite a healthy diet, you might experience deficiencies in fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) or vitamin B12.
Fatigue and Brain Fog: The gut-brain connection is powerful, and SIBO can contribute to systemic symptoms like fatigue and difficulty concentrating.
Symptoms Worsening with Probiotics or Fermented Foods: While generally beneficial, these can sometimes exacerbate SIBO symptoms by introducing more bacteria.
Beyond Symptoms: Situations Where SIBO Testing May Be Recommended
Certain underlying conditions and circumstances can increase the risk of developing SIBO. If you experience any of the above symptoms in addition to the following, discussing SIBO testing with your doctor is particularly important:
Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS): A significant overlap exists between IBS and SIBO, with many individuals diagnosed with IBS potentially having underlying SIBO.
Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) in Remission: While less common, SIBO can occur in individuals with Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis, especially during periods of remission.
Chronic Constipation or Diarrhea: Persistent and unexplained changes in bowel habits can be a red flag.
History of Abdominal Surgery: Surgeries can sometimes disrupt the normal motility of the small intestine, increasing the risk of bacterial overgrowth.
Certain Medications: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), antibiotics, and opioids can alter the gut environment and potentially contribute to SIBO.
Chronic Conditions: Conditions like diabetes, scleroderma, and hypothyroidism can affect gut motility and increase SIBO risk.
Unexplained Nutrient Deficiencies: If blood tests reveal deficiencies despite adequate dietary intake, SIBO could be interfering with absorption.
Rosacea: Interestingly, some research suggests a link between SIBO and the skin condition rosacea.
Important Considerations Before Testing
It's crucial to remember that:
Self-diagnosing is not recommended. The symptoms of SIBO can overlap with other digestive disorders.
Testing should be guided by a healthcare professional. They will consider your individual medical history and symptoms, and conduct a thorough evaluation.
The most common SIBO test is the lactulose or glucose breath test. This non-invasive test measures the levels of hydrogen and methane gases produced by bacteria in your small intestine after consuming a sugar solution.
Proper test preparation is essential for accurate results. Your doctor will provide specific instructions regarding dietary restrictions and medication adjustments before the test.
If you recognize some of these symptoms or fall into a higher-risk category, don't hesitate to discuss your concerns with your doctor or a qualified healthcare practitioner experienced in gut health. They can help determine if SIBO testing is appropriate for you and guide you through the next steps.
Understanding when to consider SIBO testing is a vital step in advocating for your gut health. By being aware of the potential signs and risk factors, you can work collaboratively with your healthcare team to uncover the root causes of your digestive discomfort and embark on a path towards a happier, healthier gut.

title: Is Olive Oil Better than Ibuprofen?
author: THE FOOD MATTERS TEAM
content:
Food is a powerful medicine. And when it comes to the silent issue of inflammation, the choices we make in our kitchens and at the grocery store can have a profound impact on our overall health and well-being.
You might be wondering, "Why all the fuss about inflammation?" Well, think of inflammation like a fire alarm in your body. When there's an injury or an infection, it's a necessary and helpful response, sending immune cells to the rescue. This is acute inflammation, and it's crucial for healing.
However, when this "alarm" keeps sounding, even when there's no immediate threat, we're dealing with chronic inflammation. This low-grade, persistent inflammation can simmer beneath the surface for years, silently contributing to a whole host of health problems, from fatigue and joint pain to more serious conditions like heart disease, type 2 diabetes, autoimmune disorders, and even some cancers.
Ignoring chronic inflammation is like ignoring a flickering engine light in your car – it might seem okay for a while, but eventually, it can lead to a major breakdown. That's why paying attention to the signals your body is sending and actively working to reduce inflammation is one of the most empowering steps you can take for long-term health.
So, how do we put out this internal fire? The answer lies largely in the incredible power of FOOD!
Think of these foods as your body's natural firefighters, packed with compounds that help to quell inflammation and support healing:
The Berry Brigade (Blueberries, Strawberries, Raspberries, Blackberries): Bursting with vibrant colors, berries are rich in anthocyanins, potent antioxidants that fight free radicals and reduce inflammation. Add them to your smoothies, yogurt, or enjoy them with this chia pudding.
Fatty Fish Friends (Salmon, Mackerel, Sardines, Tuna): These oily fish are loaded with omega-3 fatty acids (EPA and DHA), which have been extensively studied for their powerful anti-inflammatory effects. Aim for a few servings a week to reap the benefits. Make sure to try one of our all-time favorite salmon recipes here. >>
Leafy Green Heroes (Spinach, Kale, Collard Greens): Packed with vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants, dark leafy greens are nutritional powerhouses that help protect your cells from damage and reduce inflammation. Toss them in salads (like this one), sauté them, or blend them into green smoothies.
Olive Oil Oasis (Extra Virgin): Rich in oleocanthal, a natural compound with similar anti-inflammatory effects to ibuprofen, extra virgin olive oil is a healthy fat that should be a staple in your kitchen. Use it for dressings, drizzling, and light cooking.
Turmeric's Golden Touch: This vibrant spice contains curcumin, a powerful anti-inflammatory compound. Add turmeric to your curries, soups, or try a golden milk latte for a warming and healing treat. Remember that black pepper enhances curcumin absorption so grind some on top!
Ginger's Soothing Spice: With its warm and pungent flavor, ginger has long been recognized for its anti-inflammatory properties. Grate it into stir-fries, brew it into tea, or add it to your smoothies.
Nutty Allies (Almonds, Walnuts, Chia Seeds, Flax Seeds): These are good sources of healthy fats, fiber, and antioxidants, all of which contribute to reducing inflammation. Enjoy them as snacks or add them to your meals.
Avocado's Creamy Comfort: Packed with healthy monounsaturated fats, fiber, and antioxidants, avocados are a delicious and anti-inflammatory addition to your diet. Try adding them in with this delicious pasta recipe. >>
Dark Chocolate Delight (70% Cacao or Higher): Rich in flavonoids, dark chocolate can have anti-inflammatory benefits. Just remember moderation is key!
Just as some foods fight inflammation, others can fuel the fire. Limiting or avoiding these culprits can make a significant difference:
Sugary Saboteurs (Soda, Candy, Processed Sweets): High sugar intake triggers the release of inflammatory messengers in the body. Reduce your consumption of sugary drinks and processed treats.
Refined Grain Rogues (White Bread, White Pasta, Processed Cereals): These lack fiber and nutrients and can lead to rapid blood sugar spikes, promoting inflammation. Opt for whole grains instead.
Unhealthy Fat Fiends (Fried Foods, Processed Snacks): Foods high in trans fats and saturated fats (often found in fried foods and processed snacks) can contribute to inflammation. Choose healthier fats like those found in olive oil and avocados.
Processed Meat Mayhem (Hot Dogs, Sausages, Deli Meats): These often contain high levels of sodium, unhealthy fats, and additives that can promote inflammation. Choose lean, whole protein sources instead.
Excessive Alcohol Exposure: While moderate alcohol consumption might have some health benefits for some, excessive intake can trigger inflammation throughout the body.
Certain Vegetable Oils (Corn Oil, Soybean Oil, Sunflower Oil): These oils are often high in omega-6 fatty acids, and while some omega-6s are necessary, an imbalance with omega-3s can promote inflammation. Focus on olive oil and other healthier options.
Remember, taming inflammation isn't just about adding a few "superfoods" to an otherwise inflammatory diet. It's about adopting a holistic approach that prioritizes whole, unprocessed foods and minimizes those that can trigger inflammation. By making conscious choices about what you eat, you're not just nourishing your body; you're actively working to reduce inflammation, support your immune system, and protect your long-term health. title: Can Cacao Help You Give Up Alcohol, Caffeine & Other Stimulants?
author: THE FOOD MATTERS TEAM
content:
We believe in the power of nature to support our well-being. And if you're looking to gently ease away from stimulants like alcohol, caffeine, or even nicotine, cacao might just be your new best friend. It's more than just a delicious treat; it's a nutrient-rich powerhouse that can help you navigate those challenging cravings.
Stimulants work by manipulating our brain's reward system, often leading to dependence and withdrawal symptoms. When we try to cut back, our bodies crave that familiar "hit," making it difficult to stick to our goals. This is where cacao comes in, offering a natural and supportive alternative.
Cacao is packed with compounds that can help balance your brain chemistry and reduce cravings:
Theobromine: This gentle stimulant provides a sustained energy boost without the jitters and crashes associated with caffeine. It can lift your mood and improve focus, helping you stay motivated.
Anandamide: Known as the "bliss molecule," anandamide naturally elevates your mood and promotes feelings of well-being. This can help counteract the low moods often experienced during stimulant withdrawal.
Magnesium: Cacao is a rich source of magnesium, a mineral that plays a crucial role in nerve function and stress response. Magnesium deficiency can exacerbate cravings, so ensuring adequate intake is essential.
Phenylethylamine (PEA): This compound acts as a natural mood elevator, promoting feelings of happiness and contentment. It can help replace the "feel-good" sensation you might be seeking from stimulants.
Here's how you can incorporate cacao into your routine to support your journey:
Replace Caffeine with Cacao: Swap your morning coffee for a warm cacao drink. Opt for raw cacao powder or nibs to maximize the nutritional benefits.
Combat Alcohol Cravings: When cravings hit, reach for a small piece of high-quality dark chocolate (at least 70% cacao). The rich flavor and mood-boosting compounds can help curb the urge.
Support Detox: Cacao's magnesium content can support your body's natural detoxification processes, helping you eliminate toxins associated with stimulant use.
Mindful Consumption: Enjoy cacao mindfully, savoring the flavor and allowing the mood-enhancing effects to take hold. This can help you develop a healthier relationship with food and reduce reliance on external stimulants.
Cacao isn't just about curbing cravings; it's a holistic ally for your well-being. It can:
Improve mood and reduce stress.
Boost cognitive function and focus.
Support heart health.
Provide a rich source of antioxidants.
Choose high-quality, organic cacao to avoid added sugars and artificial ingredients.
Start with small amounts and gradually increase your intake as needed.
Listen to your body and adjust your consumption accordingly.
If you have any health concerns, especially concerning medications, consult with your doctor or a holistic health practitioner.
Small, consistent changes can lead to significant transformations. By incorporating cacao into your routine, you can gently support your body's natural ability to thrive, paving the way for a healthier, more balanced life. You can find our favorite ceremonial cacao HERE. >>

title: Day on a Plate of the Food Matters Holistic Nutritionist
author: THE FOOD MATTERS TEAM
content:
Hey everyone! So, you want know what a holistic nutritionist actually eats? Spoiler alert: it's not all kale smoothies and superfood powders (though I do love those!). Let me walk you through a typical day, the real, unfiltered version. My name is Kayla, and I act as the social media manager, student advisor, and holistic nutritionist here at Food Matters. Keep reading to hear what I eat in a day…
Okay, first things first: I'm a huge fan of routines. And my morning starts with... an iced decaf espresso. Yes, decaf. I know, I know. I'm sensitive to caffeine, and I've found this works best for me. Now, here's the secret weapon: collagen! I throw a scoop in there, along with some organic full cream milk (I love the richness!) and a little drizzle of maple syrup—just a teaspoon. Boom! 20 grams of protein before I even really wake up. It keeps my blood sugar stable, which is a game-changer for my energy levels.
Then, it's time for breakfast. I love a big bowl of Greek yogurt. It's so creamy and packed with protein. I top it with hemp seeds, Farmer Jo granola—seriously, it's the best—and fresh mango and berries from the farmer’s market. All those antioxidants and vitamins? My body loves it.

Lunch is where I get a little creative. Some days, it's a sourdough wrap. Sourdough is my bread of choice—easier on my digestion because it’s fermented. Inside, I pile on spinach, roasted turkey, a sprinkle of cheese, and a squirt of sriracha for a kick. Then, I pop it in the air fryer for five minutes to get it nice and crispy and enjoy it with a side of veggies. Simple and yum!
Other days, I'm craving something different. That's when I make a bowl with rice (usually brown or basmati). I add a can of wild salmon—hello, omega-3s!—avocado, pickled cucumber, and a little mayo (based on olive oil) and sriracha. It's so simple, but so satisfying.

Around 3 p.m., I start to feel that little dip. That's when I reach for a matcha latte. Matcha is my go-to for a gentle energy boost. Plus, it's packed with antioxidants. I'll usually have it with a granola bar (I try to find ones with simple ingredients) or a couple of hard-boiled eggs. Eggs are amazing! They're full of protein and good fats, and they keep me full until dinner.

Dinner is all about balance. I love a good stir-fry with lots of veggies and some kind of protein—chicken, beef, or tofu. It's quick, easy, and super nutritious. Or, if I'm feeling like something lighter, I'll make a big salad with grilled chicken or fish. And sometimes, when I have the time, I'll slow-cook something delicious with roasted vegetables—it's so comforting!

Before bed, I always have a cup of herbal tea. Chamomile, peppermint, holy basil—whatever I'm in the mood for. It's so relaxing. And sometimes, I'll have a little piece of dark chocolate or a homemade nut butter fudge.
So, that's a peek into my day on a plate. Let me remind you… what I eat is going to be different from you because what our bodies need varies. I hope that this can provide some inspiration to see that it’s not hard to make choices that nourish your body. I believe in eating real, whole foods, listening to my body's cues, and enjoying the process. Food should be fun and delicious! And remember, everyone's different. Find what works for you, and don't be afraid to experiment.

title: Foods to Eat & Avoid for Gut Health
author: THE FOOD MATTERS TEAM
content:
Here at Food Matters, we understand that true wellness begins from within. And at the very heart of your well-being lies your gut. It's a bustling ecosystem, a complex community of microbes that influence everything from your digestion to your mood. So, let's talk about how to cultivate a thriving inner garden.
Fiber-Rich Foods:
Think vibrant vegetables, luscious fruits, and hearty whole grains. Fiber is the fuel that your beneficial gut bacteria crave. It keeps things moving, promotes regularity, and fosters a diverse microbiome.
Examples: Leafy greens, berries, oats, apples, and legumes.
Fermented Foods:
These are packed with probiotics, the live microorganisms that replenish and diversify your gut flora.
Examples: Sauerkraut, kimchi, kefir, and yogurt (look for live and active cultures).
Prebiotic Foods:
These foods contain fibers that act as food for the good bacteria.
Examples: Onions, garlic, bananas, and asparagus.  (Don’t skip out on THIS delicious prebiotic tray bake.)
Polyphenol-Rich Foods:
These plant compounds act as antioxidants, and also feed beneficial gut bacteria.
Examples: Berries, dark chocolate, olives, and green tea.
Processed Foods:
These are often loaded with refined sugars, unhealthy fats, and artificial additives that can disrupt your gut balance.
Examples: Fast food, sugary drinks, and packaged snacks.
Excessive Sugar:
Sugar feeds harmful bacteria and can lead to dysbiosis, an imbalance in your gut microbiome.
Artificial Sweeteners:
Studies suggest that artificial sweeteners can negatively impact gut bacteria.
Excessive Red Meat:
Some studies suggest red meat can negatively affect the gut microbiome.
Excessive Alcohol:
Alcohol can irritate the gut lining and disrupt the balance of gut bacteria.
Remember, gut health isn't just about what you eat. It's also about how you live.
Manage stress: Chronic stress can wreak havoc on your gut.
Prioritize sleep: Quality sleep is essential for a healthy gut.
Stay hydrated: Water keeps things flowing smoothly.
By nourishing your gut with wholesome foods and embracing a balanced lifestyle, you can cultivate a thriving inner ecosystem and unlock your full potential for health and vitality. title: EFT Tapping Explained
author: THE FOOD MATTERS TEAM
content:
We're always exploring natural ways to support our health and well-being, and today we're diving into a fascinating technique called EFT tapping, or Emotional Freedom Techniques tapping. If you're searching for EFT tapping benefits or how to learn EFT tapping, you've come to the right place. We're here to break it down in a simple, Food Matters way.
What Exactly is EFT (Emotional Freedom Techniques) Tapping?
Imagine combining the ancient wisdom of acupressure with modern psychology. That's essentially what EFT tapping for anxiety and stress does. It involves tapping on specific meridian points on your body while focusing on a particular emotion or issue. These meridian points are like energy pathways, and by tapping on them, you're helping to release blockages and restore balance.
How Does it Work? (EFT Tapping Points Explained)
When we experience stress or trauma, it can get stored in our bodies as emotional energy. This can lead to feelings of anxiety, fear, or even physical discomfort. EFT tapping techniques help to release this stored energy by:
Identifying the Issue: You start by focusing on the specific emotion or problem you want to address.
Tapping the Points: You then tap on a sequence of meridian points on your face and upper body using your fingertips.
Verbal Affirmations: While tapping, you repeat phrases that acknowledge the issue and affirm your intention to release it.
The Tapping Sequence (EFT Tapping Points):
These are the EFT tapping points you can focus on to release blockages and restore balance:
Karate Chop Point: On the outer edge of your hand.
Eyebrow Point: At the beginning of your eyebrow.
Side of the Eye Point: On the bony edge of your eye.
Under the Eye Point: On the bony area under your eye.
Under the Nose Point: Just below your nose, above your upper lip.
Chin Point: In the crease of your chin.
Collarbone Point: Just below your collarbone.
Under the Arm Point: On the side of your body, about four inches below your armpit.
Top of the Head Point: On the crown of your head.
Why We Love EFT Tapping (Benefits of EFT Tapping):
It's Simple and Accessible: You can learn the technique quickly and use it anywhere, anytime.
It Addresses the Root Cause: Instead of just masking symptoms, it helps to release the underlying emotional blocks.
It Supports Emotional Well-Being: It can help to reduce stress relief with EFT tapping, anxiety, and other negative emotions.
It's a Natural Approach: It works with your body's natural energy systems.
Food Matters Tip (How to Learn EFT Tapping):
Start tapping while focusing on simple issues, like a minor annoyance or a fleeting feeling of stress. As you become more comfortable, you can explore deeper emotional issues. Remember to be gentle with yourself and listen to your body.
EFT tapping is a powerful tool for self-care, and we encourage you to give it a try! It's another way to take control of your well-being naturally. If you are searching for EFT tapping for weight loss, or EFT tapping for trauma, please remember to seek professional help when needed.

title: The Science Behind Visualization: Creating Your Reality, One Thought at a Time
author: THE FOOD MATTERS TEAM
content:
We believe in the power of nourishment – not just for the body, but for the mind and spirit too.  And one of the most potent tools for cultivating mental and emotional well-being is visualization.
While it might seem like just "positive thinking," there's actually a fascinating science behind how visualization works, and how you can harness it to create the reality you desire.
Our brains don't always distinguish between what's real and what's vividly imagined. When you visualize something, the same neural pathways are activated as if you were actually experiencing it. This is because the brain's emotional center, the amygdala, responds to imagined scenarios almost as if they were real. This is why visualizing something positive can evoke feelings of joy and excitement, while visualizing something negative can trigger anxiety and fear.
Every time you visualize a specific outcome, you're essentially strengthening the neural pathways associated with that outcome. Think of it like carving a path in a forest. The more you walk that path, the clearer and more defined it becomes. Similarly, the more you visualize your goals, the more your brain believes they are attainable, and the more likely you are to take the actions needed to achieve them.
You can read more about it in this study HERE.
Visualization can also influence your expectations. When you consistently visualize yourself succeeding, you begin to develop a strong belief in your ability to achieve your goals. This positive expectation can boost your confidence, reduce self-doubt, and motivate you to persevere even in the face of challenges.
The mind-body connection is well-established. Your thoughts and emotions can directly impact your physical health. Visualization can be a powerful tool for promoting healing and well-being. By visualizing yourself healthy and strong, you can activate your body's natural healing mechanisms and support your overall well-being.
Visualization can also be used to reduce stress and anxiety. By visualizing a peaceful and calming scene, you can activate the parasympathetic nervous system, which helps to slow down your heart rate, lower blood pressure, and promote relaxation.
Find a quiet space: Choose a place where you can relax and focus without distractions.
Get comfortable: Sit or lie down in a comfortable position.
Close your eyes: This helps to minimize external distractions and allows you to focus on your inner world.
Breathe deeply: Take a few deep breaths to relax your body and mind.
Engage all your senses: When you visualize, try to engage all your senses. Imagine what you would see, hear, smell, taste, and feel if you were actually experiencing the outcome you desire.
Be specific: The more specific you are in your visualization, the more effective it will be.
Feel the emotion: Don't just visualize the outcome; also try to feel the emotions associated with it. Imagine how you would feel if you achieved your goal.
Practice regularly: Like any skill, visualization takes practice. The more you practice, the better you will become at it.
Visualization is more than just wishful thinking. It's a powerful tool that can help you shape your reality by influencing your thoughts, emotions, and actions. By understanding the science behind visualization and practicing it regularly, you can harness its power to achieve your goals, improve your well-being, and create the life you truly desire.

title: Best Foods to Help Aid Digestion
author: THE FOOD MATTERS TEAM
content:
A happy gut is the cornerstone of overall well-being, influencing everything from nutrient absorption and immune function to mood and energy levels. So, if you're experiencing bloating, gas, or just generally feeling sluggish, it might be time to take a closer look at what you're eating.  Let's explore some of the best foods to help aid digestion and get your gut back on track.
Probiotics are live microorganisms that reside in your gut and play a vital role in digestion. They help break down food, produce essential nutrients, and support a healthy gut microbiome. Think of them as your gut's little helpers!
Yogurt (with live and active cultures): A classic source of probiotics, yogurt can be a delicious way to boost your gut health. Opt for plain, unsweetened varieties and add your own fruit or a drizzle of honey.
Kefir: Similar to yogurt, kefir is a fermented milk drink packed with probiotics. It has a slightly tangier taste and can be enjoyed on its own or added to smoothies.
Sauerkraut: This fermented cabbage is a powerhouse of probiotics and also provides beneficial fiber. Choose raw, unpasteurized sauerkraut for the best results.
Kimchi: A Korean staple, kimchi is made from fermented vegetables like cabbage and radish, and is loaded with probiotics and flavor.
Miso: A fermented soybean paste, miso is a common ingredient in Japanese cuisine and adds a rich, umami flavor to soups and other dishes. Try it in this ginger miso soup recipe.
Fiber is essential for healthy digestion. It adds bulk to your stool, making it easier to pass, and also acts as a prebiotic, feeding the beneficial bacteria in your gut.
Fruits: Apples, bananas, berries, and pears are all excellent sources of fiber. Enjoy them whole for maximum benefit.
Vegetables: Leafy greens, broccoli, carrots, and sweet potatoes are packed with fiber and other essential nutrients.
Whole Grains: Oats, quinoa, brown rice, and whole-wheat bread provide a good source of fiber.
Legumes: Beans, lentils, and chickpeas are not only high in fiber but also a great source of protein.
Chia Seeds and Flaxseeds: These tiny seeds are loaded with fiber and omega-3 fatty acids, which are also beneficial for gut health.
Ginger has been used for centuries to aid digestion and relieve nausea. It can help reduce inflammation in the gut and promote the movement of food through the digestive tract.
Fresh Ginger: Add freshly grated ginger to stir-fries, soups, or teas.
Ginger Tea: Steep ginger slices in hot water for a soothing and warming beverage.
Ginger Supplements: If you find it difficult to incorporate fresh ginger into your diet, you can also take ginger supplements.
Staying hydrated is crucial for healthy digestion. Water helps to soften stool and keeps things moving smoothly through your digestive system.
Water: Aim to drink plenty of water throughout the day.
Herbal Tea: Unsweetened herbal teas can also contribute to your fluid intake.
Enzymes help break down food into smaller particles, making it easier for your body to absorb nutrients.
Pineapple: Contains bromelain, an enzyme that helps break down protein.
Papaya: Contains papain, another enzyme that aids in protein digestion.
Try this parfait recipe as a way to incorporate both into your diet.
A healthy diet rich in probiotics, fiber, and other gut-friendly foods is essential for optimal digestion. By incorporating these foods into your daily routine, you can support a happy and healthy gut, leading to improved overall well-being. Remember to listen to your body and pay attention to how different foods make you feel. If you're experiencing persistent digestive issues, it's always best to consult with a healthcare professional. title: The History of Fad Diets and Why They Don’t Work
author: THE FOOD MATTERS TEAM
content:
Fad diets have been around for centuries, captivating millions of people with promises of rapid weight loss and “miracle” health transformations. While these diets may seem appealing in the moment, they often fall short of their promises and can even cause harm. But why do we keep falling for them? Let’s take a look at the history of fad diets, how they’ve evolved, and why they simply don’t work in the long run.
Fad diets first gained widespread attention in the early 20th century. One of the first notorious diet trends was the “Hollywood Diet” of the 1920s, which claimed to help people lose weight by consuming a liquid mix of grape juice and water. Though it promised quick weight loss, it was nutritionally imbalanced and unsustainable.
Fast forward to the 1950s, and we saw the rise of the Cabbage Soup Diet, which instructed dieters to consume large quantities of low-calorie cabbage soup for a week. The belief was that this would speed up metabolism and lead to weight loss. While it might have caused initial water weight loss, it didn’t lead to lasting fat loss, and as soon as people went back to normal eating habits, the weight came back—often with a vengeance.
By the time the Atkins Diet became popular in the 1970s, people had already begun to realize that extreme restrictions often led to temporary results at best. This low-carb, high-fat approach promised to turn the body into a fat-burning machine. And while some people did lose weight on the Atkins Diet, many experienced energy slumps, nutrient deficiencies, and long-term difficulties maintaining the diet.
In the 1980s and 1990s, diets linked to celebrities took off. The Grapefruit Diet was one such example, where dieters ate half a grapefruit before every meal, supposedly aiding in fat burning. Celebrities like Marilyn Monroe and other famous figures from the golden age of Hollywood were often associated with these extreme weight-loss regimens, which led many fans to follow suit.
Then came the South Beach Diet in the early 2000s - a low-carb, high-protein, and high-fat approach that was marketed as a more "sophisticated" version of Atkins. It gained traction, especially among those looking for a scientifically “validated” approach to weight loss. But as with other restrictive diets, many dieters found it difficult to maintain over time, and when the cycle of restriction and indulgence began, so did the inevitable weight regain.
Fast forward to today, and the landscape of fad diets has evolved to include a variety of diets… keto, low carb, high fat, carnivore, vegan… the list goes on. While some people may initially shed pounds, many diets are extreme, hard to maintain, and can lead to nutrient imbalances.
There are several reasons why these diets don’t work in the long run:
Unsustainable Restrictions: Fad diets often require extreme restrictions that make them hard to maintain. When a diet is overly restrictive, it can lead to feelings of deprivation, making it easier to give up or binge once the diet ends.
Nutrient Imbalances: Many fad diets eliminate entire food groups or severely limit intake of essential nutrients. This can lead to deficiencies in vital vitamins and minerals, which can harm your overall health in the long term.
Metabolic Adaptation: When you drastically cut calories or eliminate whole food groups, your metabolism can slow down as your body tries to conserve energy. This means you might stop losing weight, even if you're still following the diet, and you could gain weight back as soon as you return to normal eating habits.
Psychological Toll: Constant dieting and the cycle of restriction and bingeing can have negative effects on mental health, leading to stress, anxiety, and even disordered eating habits. This emotional rollercoaster can make it harder to build a healthy relationship with food and your body.
The “Yo-Yo” Effect: Most people regain the weight they lost on a fad diet—and often more—once they return to their usual eating patterns. This cyclical nature of weight loss and gain, known as “yo-yo dieting,” is not only frustrating but can also be damaging to your metabolism and self-esteem.
The key to sustainable health and wellness is adopting a balanced, whole-food-based approach that you can maintain for the long term. Rather than focusing on restriction and elimination, the best approach is one that emphasizes nutrient-dense foods that nourish your body and keep you feeling energized.
Here are some foundational principles to consider:
Focus on Whole Foods: Emphasize fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins, and healthy fats. These foods provide the nutrients your body needs without depriving you of essential elements.
Moderation, Not Extremes: Instead of cutting out entire food groups, aim for balance. Enjoy a variety of foods in reasonable portions, without guilt or shame.
Sustainable Movement: Incorporate regular physical activity into your life, whether through walking, yoga, weightlifting, or dancing. Movement that you enjoy is key to making it a lasting part of your lifestyle.
Mindful Eating: Pay attention to your body’s hunger and fullness cues, and make meals an enjoyable, nourishing experience rather than a source of stress or shame.
Prioritize Mental Health: Address the emotional and psychological aspects of eating. A healthy relationship with food starts with a healthy relationship with yourself. HERE are some things you can do for self-love.
While fad diets may promise quick fixes, they rarely deliver lasting results. The true path to health and well-being is not through extreme restrictions, but through balanced, mindful habits that nourish both body and mind. Instead of chasing after the next fad, focus on creating a sustainable, healthy lifestyle that you can maintain for years to come. Your body—and your mind—will thank you for it.

title: 10 Foods to Support Your Nervous System
author: THE FOOD MATTERS TEAM
content:
The nervous system is the body’s command center, controlling everything from your heartbeat to your thoughts. It relies on a steady supply of nutrients to function optimally, repair itself, and maintain resilience against stress. Symptoms of a run down nervous system can include trouble sleeping, bowel issues, sweating, chest pains, a racing heart, and more. By incorporating specific nutrient-rich foods into your diet, you can strengthen your nervous system, enhance mental clarity, and promote overall well-being. Here are the top foods that support a healthy and balanced nervous system.
Leafy greens like spinach, kale, and Swiss chard are rich in magnesium, a mineral critical for nervous system function. Magnesium helps regulate nerve impulses, reduce stress, and improve sleep quality—key components of a well-functioning nervous system.
Why It Works: Magnesium helps maintain the balance between excitatory and inhibitory signals in the nervous system, preventing overactivity and promoting calmness while B vitamins support the nervous system by promoting healthy nerve function, reducing stress, enhancing mood, and improving energy levels.
Get an extra dose of magnesium from the spinach in this delicious smoothie.
Fatty fish like salmon, mackerel, and sardines are high in omega-3 fatty acids, which are essential for building and maintaining the myelin sheath that protects nerve cells. Omega-3s also play a role in reducing inflammation and supporting neurotransmitter function.
Why It Works: Omega-3 fatty acids improve communication between nerve cells, enhancing cognitive function and reducing the risk of neurological disorders.
If you’re looking for a way to add more salmon into your diet, check out this Nori Crusted Salmon recipe.
Almonds, walnuts, flaxseeds, and chia seeds are packed with vitamin E, antioxidants, and healthy fats. These nutrients protect nerve cells from oxidative damage and support overall nerve health.
Why It Works: The combination of antioxidants and fatty acids helps repair and protect the nervous system, particularly in times of stress.
This Baked Plums recipe is an easy and creative way to get more almonds into your diet.
Berries such as blueberries, strawberries, and blackberries are loaded with antioxidants that combat oxidative stress and inflammation, which can damage nerve cells over time.
Why It Works: Antioxidants in berries help protect the brain and nervous system from damage caused by free radicals, enhancing memory and cognitive health.
As a fun way to get more strawberries into your diet, check out this easy strawberry cheesecake slice.
Foods like kimchi, sauerkraut, and yogurt are rich in probiotics that support gut health, which is directly linked to nervous system function through the gut-brain axis. A healthy gut can improve mood, cognitive function, and stress resilience.
Why It Works: The gut produces neurotransmitters like serotonin, which influence mood and nervous system regulation.
Avocados are rich in monounsaturated fats and B vitamins, particularly B6, which is vital for the production of neurotransmitters like serotonin and dopamine.
Why It Works: The healthy fats in avocados support the structure of nerve cells, while B6 enhances mood and mental clarity.
A quick guacamole or this avocado pesto pasta is a great way to get more of these fats and vitamins into your diet.
Whole grains like quinoa, brown rice, and oats provide a steady source of glucose, the primary energy source for the brain and nervous system. They also contain B vitamins, which are crucial for nerve repair and function.
Why It Works: Complex carbohydrates fuel the nervous system while supporting the production of energy-regulating neurotransmitters.
Check out our favorite way to eat oats HERE. https://www.foodmatters.com/recipe/superfood-oats-caramelized-banana-recipe
Dark chocolate (70% cacao or higher) contains flavonoids, magnesium, and a small amount of caffeine, which can enhance mood and reduce stress.
Why It Works: The antioxidants in dark chocolate improve blood flow to the brain and protect nerve cells from damage.
We love having a piece of good quality dark chocolate with a cup of tea or in this healthier fudge recipe.
Eggs are an excellent source of choline, a nutrient critical for producing acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter that plays a role in memory and muscle control.
Why It Works: Choline helps maintain the integrity of nerve cells and supports efficient communication between them.
Change up your breakfast game with this turmeric scrambled eggs recipe.
Herbal teas like chamomile, peppermint, and green tea contain compounds that promote relaxation and reduce nervous tension.
Why It Works: Herbal teas soothe the nervous system, improve sleep, and reduce the effects of stress on the body.
Brew a cup of tea before bed or change things up and make these triple layer chamomile brownies.

While nutrition is a cornerstone of nervous system health, it’s important to pair it with other supportive practices like regular physical activity, stress management, and adequate sleep. By nourishing your body with these nutrient-rich foods and maintaining a balanced lifestyle, you can ensure your nervous system remains resilient and functioning at its best.

title: How Your Gut Health Shapes Your Immune System
author: THE FOOD MATTERS TEAM
content:
Did you know that your gut has a profound impact on your immune health? Recent research has uncovered a powerful connection between gut health and autoimmune conditions, revealing that the state of your gut can either protect you from or predispose you to autoimmune issues. Let’s explore how this connection works and how you can support your gut to promote a balanced immune system.
Your gut is home to trillions of microbes collectively known as the gut microbiome. These bacteria, fungi, and other microorganisms play a crucial role in maintaining immune balance. In fact, approximately 70% of your immune system resides in your gut, making it a critical regulator of how your body responds to pathogens, inflammation, and even itself.
When the gut microbiome is in balance, it helps train the immune system to distinguish between harmful invaders and the body’s own cells. However, when gut health is compromised, this balance can break down, leading to chronic inflammation and the development of autoimmune conditions, where the immune system mistakenly attacks healthy tissues.
One of the key mechanisms linking gut health to autoimmune conditions is intestinal permeability, often referred to as "leaky gut."
In a healthy gut, the intestinal lining acts as a barrier, allowing nutrients to pass into the bloodstream while keeping harmful substances out. However, factors such as poor diet, chronic stress, infections, and certain medications can damage this lining, causing it to become "leaky."
When this happens, undigested food particles, toxins, and bacteria can escape into the bloodstream, triggering an immune response. Over time, this constant immune activation can lead to inflammation and the onset or exacerbation of autoimmune diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, and lupus.
Several factors influence the health of your gut microbiome and its ability to regulate immune function:
Diet: Processed foods, sugar, and artificial additives can disrupt the microbiome, while a diet rich in fiber, prebiotics, and probiotics supports gut health.
Stress: Chronic stress alters gut motility and microbiome composition, increasing inflammation.
Antibiotics and Medications: Overuse of antibiotics and certain medications can harm beneficial bacteria in the gut.
Environmental Toxins: Pesticides, heavy metals, and other toxins can damage the gut lining and disrupt microbial balance.
The good news is that you can take steps to restore gut health and reduce your risk of autoimmune conditions:
Eat a Diverse, Anti-Inflammatory Diet
Include fiber-rich foods like leafy greens, veggies, fruits, whole grains, and legumes to nourish beneficial gut bacteria.
Incorporate fermented foods such as sauerkraut, kimchi, and yogurt to introduce probiotics.
Reduce processed foods, sugar, and inflammatory fats.
Manage Stress
Practice mindfulness, yoga, or meditation to reduce stress levels.
Prioritize sleep and set aside time for relaxation.
Avoid Gut Irritants
Minimize the use of unnecessary medications and antibiotics.
Choose organic produce to reduce pesticide exposure.
Support Your Gut Barrier
Consume bone broth, rich in collagen and amino acids, to support the intestinal lining.
Include foods high in zinc and L-glutamine to promote repair of the gut lining.
Include healthy fats to help soothe any intestinal inflammation.
Consider Functional Testing
Work with a healthcare professional to assess your gut health through stool analysis or other functional tests.
The connection between gut health and autoimmune conditions underscores the importance of taking a holistic approach to wellness. By nurturing your gut microbiome and protecting your intestinal barrier, you can create a foundation for a balanced immune system and overall vitality. Remember, healing your gut is not just about managing symptoms—it’s about empowering your body to thrive.

title: 5 Vital Nutrients for Healthy Skin

While skincare routines play an important role, what you eat has a profound impact on the health and vibrancy of your skin. Vitamin C is a powerful antioxidant that plays a key role in collagen production, the protein that keeps your skin firm and elastic. It also helps protect your skin from environmental damage caused by UV rays and pollution.Benefits:
Reduces signs of aging, like wrinkles and fine lines
Brightens skin and evens out tone
Promotes faster healing of blemishes

Omega-3 fatty acids are essential fats that help maintain your skin’s moisture barrier and reduce inflammation, which can lead to redness or acne. They also support the production of healthy cell membranes, keeping your skin hydrated and supple.Benefits:
Alleviates dry, flaky skin
Reduces inflammation and redness
May improve conditions like eczema and psoriasis

Try this chia seed jam as a tasty way to add more chia seeds to your diet.

Supports the repair of damaged skin

Helps fade scars and dark spots

title: 5 Nutrients for Healthy, Vibrant Hair
author: THE FOOD MATTERS TEAM
content:
Healthy, vibrant hair isn’t just a matter of genetics or the products you use—it starts from within. The foods you eat and the nutrients you consume play a crucial role in supporting hair growth, strength, and shine. Here are the top five nutrients to focus on for luscious, resilient locks.
Biotin is perhaps the most well-known vitamin for hair health. It helps produce keratin, a key protein that makes up the structure of hair, skin, and nails.
Sources: Eggs, almonds, sweet potatoes, spinach, and bananas. (Try these sweet potato fritters!)
Tip: Include biotin-rich foods in your diet or consider a high-quality supplement if you’re experiencing thinning hair.
Vitamin D plays a role in creating new hair follicles, which are essential for new hair growth. A deficiency in this nutrient has been linked to hair loss.
Sources: Fatty fish (like salmon and mackerel), mushrooms, fortified foods, and sunlight exposure. Try this Coconut & Mackerel Crusted Salmon.
Tip: Aim for 10-15 minutes of sunlight daily to boost vitamin D levels naturally.
Iron deficiency is a common cause of hair loss, especially in women. Iron helps carry oxygen to hair follicles, supporting their growth and strength.
Sources: Grass-fed beef, lentils, spinach, and quinoa. Try this quinoa tabbouleh.
Tip: Pair plant-based iron sources with vitamin C-rich foods (like citrus fruits) to enhance absorption.
Omega-3s nourish hair follicles, promote a healthy scalp, and add shine to your strands. They also have anti-inflammatory properties that may help reduce hair thinning caused by stress or other factors.
Sources: Walnuts, flaxseeds, chia seeds, pastured eggs, and fatty fish like salmon. Try this smoothie for a way to incorporate chia seeds.
Tip: Incorporate a mix of plant-based and marine omega-3 sources for a balanced intake.
Zinc is essential for tissue growth and repair, including the repair of hair follicles. It also helps regulate oil production in the scalp, which can prevent dandruff and other scalp conditions.
Sources: Pumpkin seeds, chickpeas, oysters, and cashews. Make sure to check out this cashew chai milk.
Tip: Avoid over-supplementing zinc, as too much can interfere with the absorption of other essential minerals like copper.
While nutrients are vital, don’t overlook the basics: staying hydrated and eating enough protein. Hair is primarily made of protein, so ensure your diet includes lean meats, legumes, or plant-based protein sources.
Nourishing your hair starts with nourishing your body. By incorporating these key nutrients into your diet, you can support healthier, stronger, and more vibrant hair from the inside out.

title: How to Choose the Best Collagen Powder
author: THE FOOD MATTERS TEAM
content:
Collagen powder has become a staple in many wellness routines, celebrated for its potential benefits to skin, hair, joints, and gut health. But with so many options on the market, how can you ensure you’re selecting the best product for your needs? Here’s a guide to help you navigate the shelves with confidence.
Collagen powders come from various sources, including bovine (cow), marine (fish), porcine (pig), or even chicken.
Bovine Collagen: Derived from cows, this type is rich in type I and III collagen, which support skin, hair, nails, and bones.
Marine Collagen: Extracted from fish, it’s rich in type I collagen and often praised for its superior bioavailability (how well your body absorbs it).
Chicken Collagen: High in type II collagen, which primarily supports cartilage and joint health.
Choose the source based on your specific health goals and dietary preferences.
Some even offer a blend, to ensure amino acid diversity.
Look for products that list “hydrolyzed collagen” or “collagen peptides” as the main ingredient. These terms indicate the collagen has been broken down for easier absorption. Avoid powders with unnecessary fillers, artificial flavors, or sweeteners.
For animal-based collagen, prioritize powders sourced from grass-fed, pasture-raised cows or wild-caught fish. These labels ensure the animals were raised in humane conditions and without unnecessary exposure to hormones or antibiotics.
Some collagen powders are fortified with complementary nutrients like:
Vitamin C: Boosts collagen synthesis in the body.
Hyaluronic Acid: Supports skin hydration and elasticity.
Biotin: Promotes healthy hair and nails.
While these additions can enhance benefits, ensure they align with your health needs.
Look for certifications that signal quality and safety, such as:
Non-GMO
Gluten-Free
Third-Party Tested
These certifications provide reassurance that the product has undergone rigorous testing.
Collagen powders come in unflavored or flavored varieties.
Unflavored Collagen: Versatile and easy to mix into coffee, smoothies, or soups.
Flavored Collagen: Great for making lattes or enjoying on its own but may contain added sugars or flavors.
Start with a small serving and observe how your body responds. While rare, some people may experience digestive discomfort or allergic reactions to specific collagen sources.
Collagen is not a quick fix. To reap its benefits, consistency is key. Look for a powder that fits your routine and tastes good enough to enjoy daily.
By taking the time to evaluate your options, you can select a collagen powder that aligns with your health goals, dietary preferences, and values. title: The Importance of Weight Lifting: Building Strength for Body and Mind
author: THE FOOD MATTERS TEAM
content:
When it comes to fitness, weight lifting is often overshadowed by cardio and high-intensity workouts. However, incorporating resistance training into your routine can profoundly impact your overall health, going far beyond aesthetics. Let’s explore why weight lifting is essential for a strong body, balanced mind, and long-term well-being.
After the age of 30, we naturally begin to lose muscle mass—a process known as sarcopenia. Weight lifting helps counteract this decline by stimulating muscle growth and maintaining strength. Whether you’re lifting dumbbells, using resistance bands, or doing bodyweight exercises, building muscle supports mobility, balance, and daily functional activities.
Muscle is metabolically active, meaning it burns more calories at rest compared to fat. Regular weight lifting not only helps you build lean muscle but also increases your resting metabolic rate, making it easier to maintain a healthy weight.
Weight lifting is a form of weight-bearing exercise, which is crucial for maintaining and improving bone density. This is especially important for preventing osteoporosis and reducing the risk of fractures as we age. Resistance training stimulates bone remodeling, keeping your skeletal system strong and resilient.
Though traditionally associated with cardio, heart health benefits from resistance training too. Weight lifting enhances circulation, lowers blood pressure, and improves lipid profiles. It also supports overall cardiovascular function by reducing visceral fat—the harmful fat around your organs.
The benefits of weight lifting extend to mental health. Studies show it can reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression, boost self-confidence, and improve sleep quality. The sense of accomplishment from progressively lifting heavier weights fosters resilience and a positive mindset.
Resistance training plays a significant role in hormonal health. It helps regulate insulin sensitivity, reduce cortisol (stress hormone) levels, and boost the production of growth hormone and testosterone, which are essential for muscle repair, fat metabolism, and overall vitality.
By improving strength, balance, and coordination, weight lifting supports functional fitness—your ability to perform everyday tasks with ease. This not only enhances quality of life but also promotes independence as you age, reducing the risk of falls and injuries.
If you’re new to weight lifting, it’s essential to begin with proper guidance and realistic goals:
Start Light: Focus on form and technique with lighter weights before increasing intensity.
Mix It Up: Incorporate a variety of movements targeting different muscle groups, such as squats, deadlifts, and rows.
Schedule Rest Days: Allow time for recovery to prevent injury and support muscle repair.
Seek Professional Guidance: Work with a personal trainer or join a fitness class to ensure safe and effective workouts.
Weight lifting is more than just a fitness trend—it’s a cornerstone of a healthy, balanced lifestyle. From physical strength and metabolic health to mental well-being and longevity, the benefits of resistance training are too significant to ignore.
We believe in empowering you to take charge of your health through holistic practices. Whether you’re lifting weights at the gym or incorporating resistance bands into your home routine, the key is consistency. Start small, stay committed, and watch as you grow stronger—inside and out.

title: The Rise of Adaptogens: Nature's Answer to Modern Stress
author: THE FOOD MATTERS TEAM
content:
Adaptogens - AKA herbs and plants that help the body adapt to stress and restore homeostasis - are rising in popularity as more and more people look for natural solutions to find healthy balance in their lives. These botanical wonders have a rich history in traditional medicine systems like Ayurveda and Traditional Chinese Medicine, but their modern resurgence is no coincidence.
Adaptogens are a class of herbs and fungi that support the body's resilience to physical, emotional, and environmental stressors. They work by interacting with the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and the sympathetic nervous system, both of which are crucial in regulating stress responses.
What sets adaptogens apart from other supplements is their ability to be non-specific, meaning they work where the body needs support most. They are also non-toxic, meaning they generally have a balancing effect without overstimulation or suppression.
In recent years, adaptogens have found their way into everything from teas and smoothies to supplements and skin care products. This surge in popularity can be attributed to a few key factors:
Increased Stress and Burnout: As work demands, technological connectivity, and lifestyle pressures rise, people are looking for sustainable ways to manage stress. Adaptogens are seen as a natural, holistic approach to doing just that.
Scientific Backing: While adaptogens have been used for centuries, modern research has started to validate some of their benefits. Studies on adaptogens like ashwagandha, rhodiola, and holy basil suggest they can help lower cortisol levels, improve focus, and boost energy—benefits that many of us could use.
Integration with Wellness Trends: The rise of mindfulness, functional foods, and plant-based diets has created a fertile environment for adaptogens to take root. These herbs fit seamlessly into the growing trend of biohacking and personalized health, offering a natural alternative to pharmaceuticals.
Ashwagandha: One of the most studied adaptogens, ashwagandha, is known for its ability to reduce cortisol levels, improve sleep, and alleviate anxiety. You can dive deeper into this adaptogen here.
Rhodiola Rosea: This plant is revered for its ability to enhance mental clarity, boost stamina, and reduce fatigue, particularly in individuals under chronic stress.
Holy Basil (Tulsi): Used in Ayurveda for centuries, holy basil is considered a sacred herb with anti-inflammatory and immune-boosting properties. It's particularly effective in calming the mind and improving mood.
Reishi Mushroom: Known as the "mushroom of immortality," reishi supports the immune system, reduces inflammation, and promotes a sense of calm. If you’ve never had it before, try using it in this delicious recipe.
Schisandra: This berry is prized for its anti-fatigue properties and ability to improve concentration, making it a favorite among those looking to boost mental clarity.
Adaptogens don’t work by simply blocking the effects of stress; instead, they help the body’s systems function more efficiently. They act as modulators, restoring balance where it’s needed most. For example, if cortisol levels are too high due to chronic stress, adaptogens can help bring them down. Conversely, if cortisol is too low (leading to fatigue), adaptogens can help support its production.
This balancing effect is particularly important in today’s health climate, where the goal is not to eliminate stress entirely—an unrealistic expectation—but to improve our resilience to it.
The versatility of adaptogens makes them easy to incorporate into everyday life. They can be taken in capsule form, added to smoothies, or steeped into teas. However, it’s important to remember that adaptogens are not a quick fix. Their effects are subtle and cumulative, often requiring consistent use over weeks or months to fully experience the benefits.
When starting with adaptogens, it’s wise to consult a healthcare practitioner, especially if you are on medication or have pre-existing conditions. Adaptogens can interact with other treatments, so professional guidance ensures safe integration.
As more people seek out natural ways to support their health, adaptogens are likely to remain a staple in the wellness world. Research is ongoing, with more studies needed to explore their full range of benefits. However, as consumer interest in plant-based and functional remedies grows, adaptogens are well-positioned to meet the demand.
The rise of adaptogens is more than just a trend—it's a return to nature's wisdom, offering a holistic way to support our bodies in an increasingly demanding world. Whether you're looking to enhance mental clarity, reduce anxiety, or simply improve your overall resilience, adaptogens might just be the natural ally you've been seeking.

title: Hacks for A Healthier Holiday Season
author: THE FOOD MATTERS TEAM
content:
The holiday season is a time for celebration, connection, and indulgence—but it doesn’t have to derail your health goals. With a little intention and a few practical hacks, you can enjoy the festivities while staying aligned with your well-being. Here are our top tips for thriving this holiday season:
The choices you make in the morning can set the tone for the rest of your day. Begin with a nutrient-packed breakfast, such as a green smoothie, chia pudding, or scrambled eggs with sautéed vegetables. Adding a morning meditation or gentle movement like yoga can also help you stay centered and reduce holiday stress.
Amidst holiday feasts and celebratory drinks, it’s easy to forget to hydrate. Keep a water bottle handy and sip throughout the day. Adding a squeeze of lemon or a splash of electrolyte solution can make hydration more enjoyable and effective.
Holiday meals are often loaded with processed ingredients and sugary treats. Instead, prioritize quality, whole-food ingredients. Opt for roasted vegetables, high-quality proteins, and healthy fats. When indulging in desserts, try recipes made with natural sweeteners like honey, maple syrup, or dates.
If you’re attending a gathering, contribute a dish that aligns with your health goals. A vibrant salad, a gluten-free stuffing, or a nourishing soup can ensure there’s something wholesome on the table. Bonus: It might inspire others to make healthier choices too!
https://www.foodmatters.com/recipe/beetroot-buckwheat-and-walnut-salad
With so many tempting foods, it’s easy to overindulge. Slow down and savor every bite. Pay attention to your body’s hunger and fullness cues. Mindful eating not only enhances the enjoyment of your meal but also prevents that uncomfortable post-meal sluggishness.
Maintain a movement routine to feel better physically and mentally. If your schedule is packed, get creative: take a walk after meals, engage in a family-friendly activity like dancing or hiking, or commit to a quick 10-minute home workout.
With late-night parties and endless to-dos, sleep can take a backseat. However, getting quality sleep is essential for energy, mood, and immune function. Create a bedtime routine, limit screen time before bed, and consider using blue light-blocking glasses in the evening.
The holidays can be as stressful as they are joyful. Make time for relaxation practices like journaling, deep breathing, or a calming cup of herbal tea. Saying "no" to overwhelming commitments can also protect your mental health.
Rather than focusing on what you "can’t" have, set positive intentions for how you want to feel. This mindset encourages you to make choices that nourish your body and soul, without feelings of deprivation.
Amidst the hustle and bustle, pause to reflect on what truly matters. Cultivating gratitude can help you stay present and appreciate the season’s beauty, beyond food and gifts.

The holiday season is about connection, celebration, and joy. By incorporating these simple hacks, you can make choices that support your health while still embracing the magic of the season.
Wishing you a happy, healthy, and harmonious holiday season from all of us at the Food Matters Institute!

title: Cacao vs Ceremonial Cacao: Which is Right for You?
author: THE FOOD MATTERS TEAM
content:
The rich, complex world of cacao offers a treasure trove of wellness and flavor, but not all cacao is created equal. As cacao’s popularity grows, there is also an increasing appreciation for “ceremonial cacao”—a specific form celebrated for its historical significance, unique preparation, and transformative health benefits. Today, we’re diving into the distinctions between standard cacao and ceremonial cacao, the profound history behind ceremonial cacao, and how both can enrich modern wellness practices. In a recent podcast with Dan Koch, founder of Sacred Cacao, he even shared about how he harnessed the power of cacao to help him overcome challenges with alcohol and really tap into his inner self. The power of this bean goes far beyond what you may realize.
Cacao, often confused with cocoa, is the minimally processed product of the cacao bean, harvested from the Theobroma cacao tree. Known for its bold, earthy flavor and versatility, cacao serves as the foundation for chocolate-making, healthy beverages, and snacks. Cacao is widely recognized for its health benefits, including:
High Antioxidant Content:  Packed with polyphenols, cacao helps protect against oxidative stress, supporting heart health and reducing inflammation.
Minerals and Nutrients:  Cacao contains high levels of magnesium, iron, and potassium, crucial for muscle relaxation, blood health, and cardiovascular support.
Mood Enhancement:  Known for its natural compounds like theobromine, anandamide, and phenylethylamine, cacao has mood-boosting properties, often linked to feelings of calm, focus, and even mild euphoria.
The cacao used in most foods and supplements undergoes some processing to optimize flavor and texture, which may reduce its potency and certain beneficial compounds. In contrast, ceremonial cacao is treated with much more reverence and care, and its purpose extends far beyond taste.
Ceremonial cacao is a specific, high-grade type of cacao with roots dating back to ancient Mesoamerican cultures, particularly the Maya and the Aztecs. This cacao was, and still is, revered as sacred, often consumed in a ceremonial context to connect with nature, community, and spirituality. The cacao tree, Theobroma cacao, produces cacao in various forms, including nibs, butter, powder, and mass, which serve as the foundation of all chocolate.
Unlike most commercially processed cacao, ceremonial cacao is harvested, processed, and prepared with an intention to preserve the spirit and natural compounds of the cacao plant. Here’s what differentiates it:
Origins and Sourcing:  Ceremonial cacao is often sourced from regions where indigenous farming techniques are practiced, with special attention to soil health and ecological balance. The cacao beans are typically grown in shade, which helps preserve biodiversity. Our friends at Sacred Cacao are who we trust for top-quality ceremonial cacao.
Minimal Processing:  Ceremonial cacao is processed using traditional methods. The beans are usually fermented, sun-dried, and lightly roasted to retain more of the original phytonutrients and complex flavors. This preserves its natural oils, taste, and nutritional profile in a way that conventional cacao may not.
Intention and Respect:  The preparation of ceremonial cacao is considered a mindful process. The growers and producers approach the cultivation and crafting of this cacao with reverence, often adhering to traditional rituals and prayer. This respect for the plant and its benefits is thought to amplify the cacao’s energetic qualities.
Ceremonial cacao boasts a wealth of nutrients similar to standard cacao but in a more potent, synergistic form. Here are some of the notable health benefits:
Heart and Vascular Health:  With high concentrations of flavonoids, ceremonial cacao helps improve blood flow, supporting heart health and circulation.
Nervous System Nourishment:  Ceremonial cacao is rich in magnesium, an essential mineral that supports relaxation, stress resilience, and sleep quality. For those with stress-related tension, the relaxing effects of ceremonial cacao can offer powerful relief.
Enhanced Mental Clarity and Focus:  Ceremonial cacao is known for theobromine, a stimulant similar to caffeine but without the jittery side effects. This can boost concentration and productivity without the typical caffeine crash.
Mood and Emotional Balance:  The sacred aspect of ceremonial cacao elevates its mood-boosting potential. With a high level of anandamide, also known as the "bliss molecule," ceremonial cacao can promote feelings of joy, connectedness, and emotional openness. This quality makes it ideal for meditation and mindfulness practices.
Spiritual Connection:  In ceremonial settings, cacao is often taken with an intention, such as emotional release or gratitude. Many people report enhanced self-awareness and connection with others during ceremonial cacao rituals.
Incorporating ceremonial cacao into your wellness practice can be as simple or as involved as you’d like. Here are some popular ways to use it:
Cacao Rituals:  A cacao ceremony typically involves setting an intention and mindfully consuming cacao in a quiet, peaceful setting. Many people choose to meditate, journal, or practice gentle movement, such as yoga, to deepen the connection with themselves.
Daily Morning Drink:  For a rich start to the day, you can prepare ceremonial cacao by whisking it with hot water, a pinch of sea salt, and optional spices like cinnamon or cayenne. This simple preparation preserves the cacao’s nutrients and potent taste.
Mindful Sharing:  Ceremonial cacao can also be enjoyed as a shared experience. The ritual of preparing and drinking cacao with others can cultivate a sense of community and support.
Choosing between standard cacao and ceremonial cacao ultimately depends on your goals. If you’re primarily seeking a nutrient-rich ingredient for everyday cooking and snacks, regular cacao products will likely suit your needs. However, if you’re drawn to a deeper, more intentional experience with cacao, ceremonial cacao is a powerful choice for mindfulness, personal reflection, and physical well-being.
Cacao, in all its forms, offers impressive health benefits and a connection to ancient wisdom. While standard cacao provides many nutritional advantages, ceremonial cacao goes a step further, inviting us to slow down, set intentions, and reconnect with ourselves. Whether you choose to embrace cacao in its ceremonial form or use it in recipes and snacks, this extraordinary superfood can elevate your wellness journey, one mindful sip at a time. title: Healthy Thanksgiving Swaps for a Delicious and Nourishing Holiday
author: THE FOOD MATTERS TEAM
content:
At Food Matters, we believe that food is medicine, and every meal is an opportunity to nourish our bodies. Thanksgiving is a time for connection and celebration, but it doesn’t mean we have to sacrifice our health. By choosing whole, nutrient-dense ingredients, we can elevate classic Thanksgiving dishes to support our well-being. Here are our top healthy swaps to enjoy a fulfilling, balanced, and flavorful Thanksgiving feast.
Mashed potatoes are a holiday staple, but they’re often prepared with heavy cream and butter, making them high in calories and low in nutrients. Swap out potatoes for cauliflower and add flavor with fresh garlic, herbs like rosemary and thyme, and a drizzle of olive oil for a creamy, nutrient-packed side.
Why This Swap Matters: Cauliflower is rich in fiber, antioxidants, and vitamin C, which support immunity, digestion, and overall health. This swap offers a lighter, anti-inflammatory alternative to potatoes without sacrificing flavor.
Heavy cream may add richness to dishes, but plant-based or Greek yogurt can provide a similar creamy texture with additional nutrients. Coconut yogurt is dairy-free and offers healthy fats, while Greek yogurt adds protein and probiotics. Use these in soups, casseroles, and desserts for a balanced creaminess.
Why This Swap Matters: Probiotics from yogurt support gut health, which is fundamental to nutrient absorption and immune function. Choosing yogurt over heavy cream reduces saturated fat intake and supports digestion.
Traditional stuffing made from white bread is often high in refined carbs, spiking blood sugar and leaving us feeling sluggish. Choose whole-grain bread or wild rice for a fiber-rich, more nourishing base. Add in sautéed mushrooms, celery, onions, and plenty of fresh herbs for flavor.
Why This Swap Matters: Whole grains and wild rice offer more vitamins, minerals, and fiber than refined grains, supporting steady energy levels, better digestion, and a sense of fullness that helps prevent overeating.
This is the recipe for stuffing we like to use.
Thanksgiving desserts and sauces tend to be laden with refined sugars, which can disrupt blood sugar levels and mood. Instead, opt for maple syrup or date paste. These natural sweeteners offer vitamins, minerals, and a depth of flavor, making them a more wholesome choice in pies, sauces, and marinades.
Why This Swap Matters: Natural sweeteners have a lower glycemic impact than refined sugar and provide antioxidants and trace minerals like zinc and manganese, supporting metabolism and immune health. So you don't the get blood sugar spike and energy crash after your have your Thanksgiving meal! (And won't get sick afterwards either.)
Our go-to pumpkin pie recipe uses only unrefined sweeteners. You can get the recipe HERE.
Butter is often used liberally in Thanksgiving recipes, but coconut oil or ghee provide more beneficial fats. Coconut oil adds a slight sweetness that complements roasted vegetables, while ghee offers a rich, nutty flavor with additional vitamins and minerals and adds a depth of richness to anything you use it with!
Why This Swap Matters: Ghee and coconut oil contain healthy fats that are easily metabolized and provide sustained energy. Ghee is also rich in vitamins A, D, and E, which are essential for immune health, skin, and vision.
Traditional gravy is made with drippings and flour, but bone broth offers a richer, more nutrient-dense option. Use bone broth as the base and thicken it with a natural starch` like arrowroot powder. Add fresh herbs, garlic, and a pinch of sea salt for a flavorful, gut-supporting gravy.
Why This Swap Matters: Bone broth is rich in collagen, which supports gut health, joint flexibility, and skin integrity. Its amino acids and minerals also aid in reducing inflammation and boosting immunity, making it a perfect holiday addition.
Green bean casserole is a common side dish but often loaded with canned soup and fried onions. Try sautéing dark leafy greens like kale, Swiss chard, or collard greens in olive oil and garlic. Top with toasted nuts or seeds for added texture and flavor.
Why This Swap Matters: Dark leafy greens are among the most nutrient-dense foods, packed with vitamins A, C, and K, along with calcium and iron. They support detoxification, reduce inflammation, and add vibrant, health-supporting nutrients to your Thanksgiving meal.
With these mindful swaps, you can honor traditional Thanksgiving flavors while prioritizing health and nourishment. Each ingredient swap brings you closer to a wholefoods-based meal that supports optimal wellness without compromising taste or joy. Enjoy a Thanksgiving feast that reflects gratitude for your health and the earth’s bounty – a true celebration of all that matters.
